pr_title: KEP-3221: Implement authorization configuration file reloading
pr_body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind feature

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Implements reloading of the authorization configuration file. File reloads when an observed file event occurs or a 1 minute poll is encountered.

Best reviewed commit-by-commit, the validation / construction is refactored to split out the rbac / node / abac construction, and move the authorization construction to the reload functions.

Fixes #119102

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?
```release-note
kube-apiserver now reloads the `--authorization-config` file when it changes. Reloads increment the `apiserver_authorization_config_controller_automatic_reload_last_timestamp_seconds` timestamp metric, with `status="success"` for successful reloads and `status="failed"` for failed reloads. Failed reloads keep using the previously loaded authorization configuration.
```

cc @ritazh @palnabarun

issue_context.title: [StructuredAuthorizationConfig] Implement reloading of configuration
issue_context.body:
### What would you like to be added?

Implement reloading of configuration in a loop at defined time intervals.

- Replace active authorizer on successful load and validation pass.
- Log and metric on failure

From the KEP:
The API server will periodically reload the configuration at a specific time interval. If it or any of referenced files change, and the new configuration passes validation, then the new configuration will be used for the Authorizer chain. The reloader will also check if the webhook is healthy, thereby preventing any typo/misconfiguration with the Webhook resulting in bad Authorizer config. If healthcheck on the webhook failed, the last known good config will be used. In the next iteration of reload, if webhook is found to be healthy, the new config will be used. Logging and metrics would be used to signal success/failure of a config reload so that cluster admins can have observability over this process. Reload must not add or remove Node or RBAC authorizers. They can be reordered, but cannot be added or removed.



### Why is this needed?

Implements https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-auth/3221-structured-authorization-configuration

review_comments: is `authorizer.Name` always expected to be lowercase as well?

example reasons this could fail:
* config tries to reference an authorizer that wasn't present at server start (RBAC, etc). this will always fail if we retry with an identical config
* config references an external kubeconfig file that doesn't exist on first try; this could succeed later if they fixed up or created the kubeconfig file, but it is better to document that the authorization config should be changed last and all supporting files should be in place before it is modified.
could there be an edge case where only a webhook authorizer was specified at startup and it got removed on reload? Is that a valid case?
if they do that, it's invalid... you can't drop all authorizers

+       // initialConfig holds the ReloadFile used to initiate background reloading,
+       // and information used to construct webhooks that isn't exposed in the authorization
+       // configuration file (dial function, backoff settings, etc)
not sure how much this matters but do we need to getHash every time or can we cache it?
since this only fires when we update our metric, I don't think it happens often enough to cache... the hash is super fast
Can we write one shared controller that handles the file watching and polling that we can re-use for authn/authz/kms?
What if the kubeconfig of an authorizer changes without the main file changing?

meh... I'd _really_ like to avoid nested file watches... (authz config file → referenced kubeconfig files → referenced cert / CA files inside that)

my suggestion would be to document that updating kubeconfig file content does not trigger reload (though a reload would re-read content in the referenced kubeconfig files), and if you want to dynamically update content inside that to suggest appending a hash of the content to the kubeconfig filename to make it content-addressed and surface a change in the authz config file
What if we only watch the main authz config but check all references during the poll?

@ritazh had a good point that triggering off of changes to kubeconfig files can create race conditions or misconfigurations if users want to change something that requires modifying both the kubeconfig and authz config file, and update them in the wrong order.

I think it's probably better to use unique kubeconfig filenames for changed content and have the authz config file update to point to the new kubeconfig file be the last step that makes the change effective.
